title: Anaphylaxis (adults and children)
subject: emergency
setting: Emergency department, ward, OPD, operating theatre, prehospital
summary: Give IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh at once (0.01 mg/kg, maximum 0.5 mg; adults 500 micrograms), repeat after 5 minutes if needed, lie the patient flat, give oxygen and IV fluid for shock, and start a low-dose adrenaline infusion if two doses fail. Antihistamines and steroids are not first-line.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Sudden airway (swelling, stridor, hoarseness), breathing (wheeze, hypoxia) or circulation (hypotension, collapse) problems after a trigger, usually with skin or mucosal changes; skin signs can be absent.

WAO criteria: acute skin or mucosal involvement plus respiratory compromise, hypotension or severe GI symptoms; OR acute hypotension, bronchospasm or laryngeal involvement after exposure to a known or likely allergen, even without skin signs.
Common triggers: drugs (beta-lactams, NSAIDs, contrast media, anaesthetic agents, snake antivenom, equine anti-rabies serum), insect stings, foods (peanut, tree nuts, shellfish, wheat).
Differentials: vasovagal syncope, panic attack, acute asthma, sepsis, and ACE inhibitor or hereditary angioedema (bradykinin-mediated, does not respond to adrenaline).

sections.title: Immediate treatment
items: Call for help, stop or remove the trigger (drug infusion, antivenom, blood product) and assess ABCDE.

IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL into the anterolateral mid-thigh immediately: adult and child over 12 years 500 micrograms (0.5 mL); 6 to 12 years 300 micrograms (0.3 mL); 6 months to 6 years 150 micrograms (0.15 mL); under 6 months 100 to 150 micrograms. Weight-based: 0.01 mg/kg, maximum 0.5 mg.
Repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if airway, breathing or circulation problems persist.
Position: lie flat with legs raised; semi-recumbent if breathing is difficult; recovery position if unconscious; left side if pregnant. Never let the patient stand or walk during the reaction.
High-flow oxygen, then titrate to SpO2 94 to 98%.
Hypotension or poor response to the first dose: IV or IO crystalloid bolus, 500 to 1000 mL in adults and 10 mL/kg in children; repeat as needed (adults may need 3 to 5 L). Stop any colloid infusion.
Persistent bronchospasm after adrenaline: nebulised salbutamol and/or ipratropium. Nebulised adrenaline is only an adjunct for upper airway obstruction.

sections.title: Refractory anaphylaxis
items: Refractory: respiratory or cardiovascular features persist despite 2 appropriate doses of adrenaline. Get critical care help; keep giving IM adrenaline every 5 minutes until an infusion is running.

Low-dose IV adrenaline infusion: 1 mg in 100 mL 0.9% saline (10 micrograms/mL) by pump via a dedicated line; start 0.5 mL/kg/h (about 0.1 microgram/kg/min), or 1 mL/kg/h if hypotensive or hypoxic; titrate. A peripheral cannula or IO is acceptable initially.
IV adrenaline boluses (adult 50 micrograms, child about 1 microgram/kg) only by specialists experienced in vasopressor titration. Never give undiluted 1 mg/mL adrenaline IV.
Continue crystalloid resuscitation; if refractory to adrenaline infusion, add a second vasopressor (noradrenaline, metaraminol or vasopressin) per local protocol.
On a beta blocker and not responding to adrenaline and fluids: consider glucagon.
Consider hydrocortisone after initial resuscitation for refractory reactions or ongoing asthma or shock; it must not delay adrenaline.
Cardiac arrest: standard ALS (adrenaline 1 mg IV), aggressive fluids, and consider prolonged resuscitation.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Mast cell tryptase: first sample as soon as feasible without delaying treatment, second at 1 to 2 hours (no later than 4 hours) after onset, third at least 24 hours after resolution for a baseline. Record the sample times.
A normal tryptase does not exclude anaphylaxis, especially food-induced reactions.
During treatment: continuous ECG and SpO2, BP at least every 5 minutes; watch for adrenaline excess (tachycardia, arrhythmia, marked hypertension).

sections.title: Observation and discharge
items: Fast-track discharge after 2 hours from resolution is possible if: good response within 5 to 10 minutes to one dose given within 30 minutes of onset, complete resolution, unused auto-injectors with training, and adequate supervision at home.
Observe at least 6 hours after resolution if 2 doses of IM adrenaline were needed or there was a previous biphasic reaction.

Observe at least 12 hours after resolution if: more than 2 doses needed, severe asthma or severe respiratory compromise, possible continuing absorption (slow-release drug), late-night presentation, or poor access to emergency care.
Biphasic reactions occur in about 5% (median around 12 hours): give written advice to return immediately if symptoms recur.

Before discharge: stand the patient up to check for postural hypotension; prescribe 2 adrenaline auto-injectors where available with training, give an allergy action plan, advise trigger avoidance and refer to an allergy specialist.

sections.title: Children, pregnancy and specific settings
items: Children: IM doses by age as above; give 300 micrograms to a small or prepubertal child over 12 years; fluid boluses of 10 mL/kg. Pallor after 2 to 3 doses may be vasoconstriction; a raised BP suggests adrenaline excess.
Pregnancy: same adrenaline dose; left lateral position; treat maternal hypotension aggressively to protect the fetus.
Snake antivenom reaction: stop the infusion, give IM adrenaline, and once recovered restart antivenom slowly, because the envenoming still needs treatment.
Perioperative anaphylaxis (neuromuscular blockers, antibiotics, chlorhexidine): follow the anaesthetic anaphylaxis algorithm and refer for allergy testing with full records.
Beta blockers and ACE inhibitors can worsen severity; never withhold adrenaline because of them.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Giving an antihistamine or steroid instead of, or before, adrenaline. Antihistamines do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems.
Giving adrenaline subcutaneously or as an undiluted IV bolus; IM thigh injection is the default.
Sitting up or standing a hypotensive patient.
Discharging without adrenaline, an action plan, biphasic-reaction advice or allergy referral.

drugs.name: Adrenaline (epinephrine) 1 mg/mL IM
drugs.dose: 0.01 mg/kg IM (maximum 0.5 mg): adult and over 12 years 500 micrograms; 6 to 12 years 300 micrograms; 6 months to 6 years 150 micrograms; under 6 months 100 to 150 micrograms. Repeat after 5 minutes if needed

drugs.name: Adrenaline IV infusion (refractory)
drugs.dose: 1 mg in 100 mL 0.9% saline; start 0.5 mL/kg/h (about 0.1 microgram/kg/min), 1 mL/kg/h if severe; titrate
drugs.notes: Adults and children. Wean to 50% as symptoms improve; taper over 30 minutes starting 1 hour after resolution.

drugs.name: Crystalloid (0.9% saline, Ringer lactate, Plasma-Lyte)
drugs.dose: Adult 500 to 1000 mL IV bolus; child 10 mL/kg IV bolus; repeat as needed

drugs.name: Glucagon
drugs.dose: Adult 1 mg IV, repeat or infuse 1 to 2 mg/h; child 20 to 30 micrograms/kg IV (maximum 1 mg), repeat every 5 minutes
drugs.notes: Refractory anaphylaxis in patients on beta blockers. Causes vomiting and hyperglycaemia.

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone
drugs.dose: Adult 200 mg IV; child 4 mg/kg IV (maximum 200 mg)
drugs.notes: Refractory reactions or ongoing asthma/shock only, after initial resuscitation. Not routine.

drugs.name: Salbutamol (nebulised)
drugs.dose: Adult 5 mg; child under 5 years 2.5 mg, 5 years and over 5 mg; repeat as needed

drugs.name: Cetirizine (oral)
drugs.dose: Adult and 12 years or over 10 to 20 mg; 6 to 11 years 5 to 10 mg; 2 to 6 years 2.5 to 5 mg; under 2 years 250 micrograms/kg
drugs.notes: Skin symptoms only, after stabilisation; preferred over sedating chlorphenamine.
